For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

GPT-3 achieved $>$ 90% accuracy on the in-distribution test set for only 5 out of 29 rule functions, suggesting it did not innately use our simple intended classification rules (Appendix 4). We tried various strategies to align GPT-3’s classification behavior with our set of known rules: - Prompt iteration: We iterated on the prompt multiple times to find the clearest phrasing of the task from the model’s point of view (Appendix B.2.2). - Few-shot examples: We varied the number of few-shot examples in the prompt from 2 to 128 to measure the effect of providing more demonstrations of the pattern (Appendix B.2.3). - Meta-learning: We tried pre-pending up to 5 solved classification tasks to the prompt (the maximum possible) to provide more demonstrations of the task (Appendix B.2.4). - Chain-of-thought: We prompted the model to provide reasoning steps before predicting the label which has historically increased performance on a wide range of tasks (Appendix B.2.5). - Single-token words: We only used words which are encoded as single-tokens to control for any unintuitive effects Byte-Pair Encoding may have on classification accuracy (Appendix B.2.6).
